contexts.mrk-10-27: An answer to disciples left stunned after the conversation with the rich young man, who asked who then could possibly be saved.
contexts.luk-1-37: Said by the angel to Mary in a conversation about her elderly relative Elizabeth expecting a child. It is an argument, not a general comfort.
contexts.luk-6-37: From the Sermon on the Plain, Luke's version of the Sermon on the Mount. It is shorter and addressed directly to the listeners.
contexts.luk-10-41: Said to Martha, who has taken guests in and is handling the meal alone while her sister sits and listens. She has complained out loud.
contexts.luk-12-7: The argument rests on cheapness: sparrows were the poorest people's smallest food, five birds for two coins.
contexts.luk-15-20: From the parable of the prodigal son. The father runs to meet him, which for an older man of that time was undignified, and the listeners knew it.
contexts.luk-23-34: Said from the cross, about the people dividing his clothes at that moment. It is the first of the seven sayings spoken at the crucifixion.
contexts.jhn-1-5: From the Gospel's prologue, written as a hymn. The verb can mean both 'did not grasp' and 'did not overcome'; translators have to choose one.
contexts.jhn-8-12: Said in the temple court during the feast of tabernacles, when huge lamps burned there all week. The image was right in front of the listeners.
contexts.jhn-10-10: From the discourse about the shepherd and the hired hand, said after a healed blind man was thrown out of the synagogue for refusing to recant.
contexts.jhn-11-35: The shortest verse in the Gospels. Jesus weeps at Lazarus' tomb knowing that within minutes he will call him out alive.
contexts.jhn-13-34: Said at the table, right after he washed the disciples' feet, a job done in a household by the lowest slave.
contexts.jhn-15-13: Said the night before the arrest, on the way from the upper room. Within hours the words become a description of what happens to him.
contexts.jhn-16-33: The last line of the farewell discourse, before the prayer and the walk to the garden where he is arrested. Trouble is promised plainly, without softening.
contexts.act-20-35: Paul says goodbye to the elders of Ephesus knowing he will not see them again. He quotes a saying of Jesus found in no Gospel.
contexts.rom-5-8: Paul builds the argument backwards: he has just observed that hardly anyone would die even for a good man.
contexts.rom-12-2: The start of the letter's practical half, after eleven chapters of argument. From here Paul turns to what to do.
contexts.rom-12-12: From a list of short instructions running one after another without connectives. Affliction appears in it as a given, not a possibility.
contexts.rom-15-13: A blessing at the end of a letter to a community where Jews and gentiles could not agree about food and festivals.
contexts.1co-10-13: Said to Corinthians who considered themselves spiritually advanced. Just before, Paul reminded them how the self-assured died in the desert.
contexts.1co-13-4: Written not for weddings but in the middle of sorting out quarrels in a community split into factions arguing whose spiritual gift mattered most.
contexts.2co-1-3: The opening of a letter where Paul will soon write that in Asia he despaired even of life. He describes comfort as something passed on.
contexts.2co-4-16: Paul writes this having just listed beatings, shipwrecks and hunger. The 'light affliction' is his own assessment of his own list.
contexts.2co-5-17: From a letter to a community that had known Paul before his conversion, as a persecutor. The claim about newness applied first of all to himself.
contexts.gal-5-22: The list comes straight after a catalogue of the strife and envy occupying the community. It is singular: one fruit, not nine.
contexts.eph-2-8: From a letter to a city famous for the temple of Artemis and the amulet trade, where religion was a service you paid for.
contexts.eph-3-20: The end of the prayer with which Paul closes the letter's first half. The practical part starts next; this is the hinge.
contexts.eph-6-10: The armour image is taken from a Roman soldier, a daily sight in the port of Ephesus. Paul wrote it while in the custody of such men.
contexts.php-1-6: Paul writes to a community he founded himself and which sent him money while he was in prison. This is a thank-you letter.
contexts.php-2-3: Said to a community where, as the letter's end shows, two women had quarrelled badly enough that Paul named them in public.
contexts.php-4-8: It comes right after the advice not to be anxious. Paul suggests not suppressing thoughts but replacing them, and lists what with.
contexts.col-3-23: Said in a section on household duties, with the nearest lines addressed to slaves. The listeners were people with no choice of work.
contexts.1th-4-13: The community had buried its first dead and was at a loss. Paul does not forbid grief; he distinguishes grief with hope from grief without it.
contexts.2ti-1-7: Paul's last letter, written awaiting execution to the young Timothy, who was left leading a community and, judging by the text, was afraid.
contexts.heb-4-16: The letter is addressed to people used to a temple where only a priest approached the holy place, once a year. Hence the word 'boldness'.
contexts.heb-12-1: A stadium image: the witnesses in the stands are the people listed in the previous chapter, who died without seeing what was promised.
contexts.heb-13-5: A quotation from Moses' final speech, cited in a letter to people whose property, as the text says earlier, had been seized because of their faith.
contexts.jas-1-2: A letter to Christians scattered across the empire. James does not say trials are pleasant; he says what to do with them.
contexts.jas-1-5: It comes right after the words about trials: the wisdom needed is not general but for making sense of a particular hard situation.
contexts.jas-5-16: Said to a community where, judging by the letter, flattering the rich and despising the poor was normal. Confession is proposed as mutual.
contexts.1pe-4-10: Peter writes to Christians their neighbours treated as outsiders. The advice to serve one another is given to a community with no support from outside.
contexts.1jn-1-9: A letter to a community where some claimed they had no sin at all. This is an objection to them, not a general rule.
contexts.1jn-4-18: The fear in question is fear of punishment, as the line itself says. It is not a promise of fearlessness in general.
contexts.rev-3-20: Said to the church in Laodicea, a wealthy city with poor water piped in by aqueduct and arriving lukewarm. Hence the image.
contexts.gen-2-18: The first thing the Bible calls not good is not sin but being alone. Said before anything broke, when everything else had been called good.
contexts.gen-3-9: The first question God asks a human being in the Bible. Adam has already hidden, and the question sounds less like a search than a call out of hiding.
contexts.gen-12-1: Abram is seventy-five and is told to leave the city where he has lived his whole life, without being told where to. He learns the destination on the way.
contexts.gen-15-5: Abram is already old and childless, and has just said so aloud. He is taken outside at night and told to count the stars.
contexts.gen-16-13: These are the words of Hagar, a pregnant slave who has run into the desert from her mistress. She is the first person in the Bible to give God a name.
contexts.gen-32-26: Jacob wrestles through the night at a ford, the eve of meeting the brother he cheated twenty years earlier. He will leave that night limping.
contexts.gen-39-2: Said of Joseph during the period when he was a slave in a foreign country, sold by his own brothers. The word 'success' appears exactly here.
contexts.exo-3-14: Moses asks what to say if people ask for a name. The answer is built on the verb 'to be', and each edition renders it in its own way.
contexts.exo-34-6: Said right after the golden calf, when Moses had cut new tablets to replace the ones he broke. Prophets and psalms later quote this formula.
contexts.lev-19-18: A line from a code of everyday rules about harvests, weights and courts. Jesus later calls it the second greatest commandment, lifting it out of that list.
contexts.num-23-19: Spoken by Balaam, a diviner hired to curse Israel. He tries three times and three times says a blessing instead.
contexts.deu-8-3: Moses explains what the forty desert years were for. Jesus will quote this same line answering the first temptation — also in a desert, also hungry.
contexts.deu-30-19: Moses sets a choice before the people in his final speech and calls heaven and earth as witnesses — a legal treaty formula of the period.
contexts.deu-31-8: Said to Joshua in front of the whole people. Moses hands over leadership publicly so everyone sees the successor — and says he will not walk out front alone.
contexts.jos-1-8: Said to a new leader on his first day. The verb rendered 'meditate' means to mutter aloud in Hebrew: texts then were not read silently.
contexts.jdg-6-12: This is what Gideon is called at the moment he is threshing wheat in a winepress, hiding from raiders. He immediately objects that it must be a mistake.
contexts.rut-1-16: Spoken by Ruth, a foreign woman widowed young. She refuses to go home and leaves with her mother-in-law for a country where she will be an outsider.
contexts.1sa-3-10: Samuel is about twelve here and has three times mistaken the voice for that of the old priest. It was the priest who taught him this reply.
contexts.1sa-17-47: Spoken by a teenager with no armour to a fully armed man, in front of two armies that had stood facing each other for forty days without moving.
contexts.1sa-30-6: David's town is burned, his men's families carried off, and his own soldiers are talking about stoning him. There is help from no one.
contexts.1ki-18-21: Elijah addresses the people on Mount Carmel, where everyone has gathered. The text says they did not answer him a word.
contexts.2ki-6-16: The city is surrounded by an army and the prophet's servant is panicking. Elisha asks that his eyes be opened, and he sees what he could not a minute before.
contexts.1ch-16-11: From the song sung the day the ark was finally brought into Jerusalem, after a three-month pause caused by a fatal accident on the road.
contexts.2ch-7-14: Said to Solomon at night after the temple's dedication. The promise is conditional and addressed to a specific people in a specific land, not to any reader.
contexts.ezr-3-12: The foundation of the second temple is laid. The young shout for joy, the old weep because they remember the first, and the two sounds could not be told apart.
contexts.neh-6-3: An answer to opponents who invited Nehemiah to talks four times to pull him off the building site. He gives the same reply all four times.
contexts.est-4-14: Mordecai writes this to Esther, a queen hiding her origin. Coming to the king uninvited meant death, and she knew it.
contexts.job-1-21: Job says this on the day four messages arrived one after another: livestock stolen, servants killed, and all ten of his children dead under a collapsed house.
contexts.job-23-10: Job has just said he looks for God and finds him neither ahead nor behind. The line about being known follows straight after admitting he himself sees nothing.
contexts.psa-3-5: The heading places this psalm when David was fleeing his own son, who had raised a revolt. He writes that he slept while being hunted.
contexts.psa-8-3: A psalm of David written, by the look of the text, at night under open sky. The question about humanity is asked against the stars, not in a temple.
contexts.psa-13-1: The psalm opens with four 'how long' questions in a row. It is a direct complaint about silence, not a pious reflection on it.
contexts.psa-20-7: A psalm sung before an army marched out. Chariots and horses were then what tanks are now, and Israel had almost none of them.
contexts.psa-22-1: A psalm of David that opens with a cry of abandonment. Jesus speaks this line from the cross, and those listening knew how the psalm ends.
contexts.psa-25-4: An acrostic on the Hebrew alphabet: each line starts with the next letter. The request about the way and the request for forgiveness stand side by side.
contexts.psa-31-15: The psalm of a man who writes that he is forgotten like the dead and hears whispering around him. The words about time are said from that position.
contexts.psa-34-8: The invitation is built on taste, the most bodily of the senses. The psalm was written after David barely escaped by pretending to be insane.
contexts.psa-40-1: A psalm of David about being pulled out of a muddy pit. The word rendered 'patiently' literally means 'waited and waited'.
contexts.psa-46-10: The line sits in a psalm where the earth gives way and spears are broken. The Hebrew verb here is closer to 'let your hands drop' than to 'be quiet'.
contexts.psa-61-2: David writes that he calls from the end of the earth when his heart is faint. He asks not for strength but to be lifted higher than he can climb.
contexts.psa-68-6: A processional psalm sung as the sanctuary was carried. The line about orphans and the lonely appears in a list of what God attends to first.
contexts.psa-71-9: An old man's psalm: he writes that he has trusted God since his youth and asks not to be dropped now, as strength runs out. It is a prayer about old age.
contexts.psa-77-11: The psalm of a man who cannot sleep and asks whether God has forgotten to be merciful. He turns to remembering the past because the present tells him nothing.
contexts.psa-86-11: A request for an undivided heart — literally to stop wanting opposite things at once. The psalm is written in danger from violent men.
contexts.psa-88-18: The only psalm that ends without relief: darkness is the last word. It arrives at no comfort at all, and that has been left as it stands.
contexts.psa-102-17: The heading calls this the prayer of an afflicted person pouring out their trouble. The writer says he sits alone like a bird on a roof.
contexts.psa-112-7: An acrostic about a person who lives honestly. The line does not promise there will be no bad news; it is about how it is met.
contexts.psa-113-7: A psalm from the Passover cycle. The image is literal: the poor of that time sat in the dust by the gates and on rubbish heaps outside town.
contexts.psa-118-6: The last psalm of the Passover Hallel, sung at the end of the Passover meal. The speaker is a man who was surrounded on every side and came out alive.
contexts.psa-119-71: A line from the acrostic about the law. The writer speaks of his own trouble in the past tense: he is assessing it from the far side.
contexts.psa-122-1: A song of ascents about the moment of arrival. Pilgrims walked for days, and the joy here is that their feet are finally standing in the gates.
contexts.psa-125-2: A song of ascents. The image is literal: Jerusalem stands in a ring of hills, and pilgrims saw them the whole way up.
contexts.psa-131-2: The shortest of David's psalms. The image is precise: a weaned child no longer demands milk and simply lies beside its mother.
contexts.psa-134-1: The last song of ascents, addressed to those on night duty in the temple. Departing pilgrims sang it to the watchmen who stayed.
contexts.psa-137-1: Written in the Babylonian exile. The captives were asked to sing one of their songs for entertainment; the psalm is about refusing.
contexts.psa-139-7: David runs through places where one might hide: the heavens, the grave, the far side of the sea. The list is drawn up as an attempt, not as comfort.
contexts.psa-141-3: An evening prayer of David. He asks for a guard to be set over his own mouth — that is, over what he cannot govern himself.
contexts.psa-142-4: The heading places this psalm when David was hiding in a cave. He writes that he looks to his right and sees no one who knows him.
contexts.psa-146-5: The psalm warns against relying on princes, because their breath goes out and their plans die the same day. The advice is practical, not poetic.
contexts.pro-11-25: From a collection of short sayings. The image is agricultural: generosity is described as watering, in which the one watering also gets wet.
contexts.pro-12-25: An observation that anxiety physically weighs a person down. The remedy named is simple and available to anyone: a good word.
contexts.pro-15-1: A saying from a court collection: such rules were gathered for people who would have to speak with kings and conduct negotiations.
contexts.pro-24-16: Seven in Hebrew counting is not an exact number but 'any number of times'. The line describes not being faultless but being able to get up.
contexts.pro-27-17: A forge image: iron is set right by iron, and the process is loud and throws sparks. The saying is not about agreement but about friction.
contexts.pro-29-25: The 'snare' here is a hunter's trap for birds. The saying is about fear of people, not fear of danger.
contexts.ecc-9-11: The author lists it out: the swift do not always win the race, the wise are not always fed. It is an observation that cuts against the rest of Proverbs.
contexts.ecc-12-13: The closing lines of a book that has called everything vapour. The conclusion is short and deliberately modest, after twelve chapters of trying options.
contexts.sng-8-6: From a book that never mentions God and consists entirely of two lovers speaking. A seal on the heart is an image of ownership, not of ornament.
contexts.isa-1-18: Said at the book's opening, right after an accusation that sacrifices are offered while the poor are crushed. The crimson dye of that time did not wash out.
contexts.isa-9-2: Said of the northern districts that Assyria devastated first. Matthew's Gospel later applies this line to the start of the ministry in Galilee.
contexts.isa-35-3: Addressed not to the strong but to those meant to hold others up: strengthen someone else's hands, speak to someone else's heart. The task is handed to people.
contexts.isa-40-11: It comes straight after lines about the power that holds waters and mountains. The image shifts scale abruptly: the same one carries lambs in his chest fold.
contexts.isa-42-3: A cracked reed and a smouldering wick are things normally just thrown away. The line describes how the Lord's servant will handle them.
contexts.isa-46-4: Said in contrast to Babylonian idols, carried on shoulders at festivals. Here it is reversed: not the god is carried but the person, and into grey hair.
contexts.isa-49-15: An answer to a people who said they had been forgotten. The prophet takes the most impossible comparison available and says even it falls short.
contexts.isa-50-4: From a servant song. Knowing how to sustain the weary is described as something taught morning by morning, like a craft rather than a gift.
contexts.isa-54-10: Said to a people after catastrophe, in a chapter calling Jerusalem an abandoned wife. Mountains are taken as the image of the most stable thing a person knows.
contexts.isa-58-11: The promise is conditional: before it stands a demand to feed the hungry and shelter the homeless. The watered garden is the reward for that, not for fasting.
contexts.jer-1-5: Jeremiah answers that he is too young and cannot speak. The work he is called to will last forty years and bring him no success.
contexts.jer-6-16: Said at a fork in the road: the prophet advises stopping and asking about the ancient paths. The text says the people answered that they would not walk in them.
contexts.jer-32-17: Jeremiah prays under guard in a besieged city, having just bought a field that the Babylonians are about to occupy.
contexts.jer-33-3: Said to a prophet confined in the courtyard of the guard, unable to leave. The promise concerns things he does not yet know.
contexts.lam-3-26: From the lament over ruined Jerusalem. The word rendered 'good' stands beside 'quietly' — the advice is about waiting without words.
contexts.ezk-34-16: Said in a chapter where the shepherds are the rulers who fed themselves instead of the flock. The promise comes as their replacement, not as general comfort.
contexts.ezk-37-3: The question is asked in the middle of a valley full of dry bones. Ezekiel answers not 'yes' but 'you know' — and that is the only honest answer available.
contexts.dan-6-10: The decree is already signed and prayer is banned on pain of death for thirty days. Daniel opens his windows and prays as usual, three times a day.
contexts.jol-2-13: Tearing one's clothes was the accepted sign of grief, visible to everyone. The prophet proposes instead something no one will see.
contexts.amo-5-24: Said to people whose worship was in perfect order. The prophet says he cannot bear to listen to their songs, and demands something else instead.
contexts.jon-2-2: Jonah prays from inside the fish, where he ended up running from an assignment. He had asked the sailors to throw him into the sea himself.
contexts.mic-7-8: Said in a chapter where the prophet complains that no honest people are left and even household members cannot be trusted. The line about falling follows that.
contexts.nam-1-7: The book is entirely about the fall of Nineveh, capital of an empire that had ravaged half the known world. The line about refuge sits inside that prophecy.
contexts.hab-2-3: An answer to a prophet who took his post and demanded an explanation. He is told to write the vision large enough to be read on the run.
contexts.zec-4-6: Said to a man who has to finish a temple with a handful of returned exiles. The prophet then asks who despises the day of small beginnings.
contexts.mal-3-10: The one place where a test is invited: the prophet says 'put me to the test'. Said to people who were bringing diseased animals as offerings.
contexts.mat-4-4: The answer to the first temptation, after forty days without food. Jesus quotes Deuteronomy — words said to a people also in a desert, also about hunger.
contexts.mat-6-21: From the Sermon on the Mount. The order is the reverse of what is expected: treasure is named as the cause and the heart as the effect, not the other way round.
contexts.mat-6-33: It stands in the middle of a talk about food and clothing, addressed to people who owned one cloak. It is not about ambition but about subsistence.
contexts.mat-9-36: Said of the crowd Jesus saw while going through the towns. The Greek verb here means a physical clench inside, not sympathy in general.
contexts.mat-14-27: Night, the middle of the lake, the boat battered by waves for hours. The disciples are crying out in fear, taking the figure coming towards them for a ghost.
contexts.mat-16-24: Said after Peter tried to talk him out of dying. The listeners saw crosses along the roads and understood the image literally.
contexts.mat-25-40: From a scene of judgement where both sides are equally surprised. Neither group knew whom they had actually been helping, or failing to help.
contexts.mat-26-39: Said in a garden at night, face to the ground, hours before the arrest. Just before, he tells the disciples his soul is sorrowful to the point of death.
contexts.mrk-1-35: The day before had been a long one of healings, with the whole town at the door until night. He gets up before dawn and leaves alone; the disciples go looking.
contexts.mrk-4-39: A storm on the lake, the boat swamping, and he is asleep in the stern. The disciples wake him by asking whether he cares that they are drowning.
contexts.mrk-5-34: Said to a woman who had bled for twelve years. By law she was unclean and had no right to touch anyone, which is why she came up from behind.
contexts.mrk-6-31: Said to disciples back from their first trip out alone. The reason is given right there: so many people were coming and going that they had no time to eat.
contexts.mrk-12-41: Jesus sits opposite the treasury watching people put money in. He measures not the amount given but how much the giver had left afterwards.
contexts.luk-2-10: Said to shepherds in a night field — men whose work made them ritually unclean and who were invited nowhere.
contexts.luk-5-16: The more people gathered, the more often he withdrew. Luke notes it not as an exception but as a standing habit.
contexts.luk-7-13: Said to a widow burying her only son. She was left without a single man in the household, which in that time meant destitution.
contexts.luk-12-15: An answer to a man who asked him to settle an inheritance dispute with his brother. Jesus refuses to be the judge and talks about something else entirely.
contexts.luk-12-32: The phrase 'little flock' is about size: the listeners were few and knew it. Said right after the talk about food and clothing.
contexts.luk-17-5: The apostles ask for more faith right after being told to forgive seven times a day. The answer about a mustard seed is about size, not quantity.
contexts.luk-18-1: The introduction to a parable about a widow who kept going to a corrupt judge until he gave in. Luke states outright what the parable is for.
contexts.luk-19-10: Said in the house of Zacchaeus, a tax collector the whole town considered a traitor. The crowd outside was grumbling that he had gone in to such a man.
contexts.luk-24-32: Two disciples were walking out of Jerusalem discussing the execution and did not recognise their companion. They realised who he was only after he vanished.
contexts.jhn-4-14: Said at a well at midday to a Samaritan woman who came for water in the hottest hour to avoid meeting the other women of the village.
contexts.jhn-6-35: Said the day after he fed five thousand. The crowd came back, and he says plainly that they are looking not for a sign but for food.
contexts.jhn-9-25: Spoken by a man blind from birth, under interrogation designed to extract a particular answer. He refuses to argue theology and holds to what he knows.
contexts.jhn-12-24: Said days before the execution, when some Greeks asked to see him. His answer is not about the meeting but about what must happen to him.
contexts.jhn-14-1: The opening line of the farewell discourse, said immediately after he warned Peter about the denial. The disciples at that moment are shaken.
contexts.jhn-15-5: Said on the way to the garden, possibly past vineyards outside the city. The image was literal: a branch off the vine does not last a day.
contexts.jhn-16-22: Jesus compares what is coming to childbirth: the pain is neither cancelled nor shortened, but stops being the main thing once it is over.
contexts.jhn-21-17: Peter denied him three times at a fire in a courtyard, and is now asked three times at another fire, on a shore. The restoration matches the count of the denials.
contexts.act-4-13: This is how the ruling council, an educated body hearing their case, describes Peter and John. The word means not stupid but unschooled.
contexts.act-16-25: Paul and Silas had been beaten with rods and locked in the inner prison with their feet in stocks. It is midnight, and the other prisoners are listening.
contexts.act-17-28: Paul is speaking in Athens before philosophers and quotes not Scripture but a Greek poet, because these listeners had never read the Scriptures.
contexts.rom-3-23: The conclusion of a long argument in which Paul showed that gentiles and Jews are in the same position. The word 'all' here is the result of a proof.
contexts.rom-8-1: It comes straight after a chapter where Paul describes doing what he does not want and calls himself a wretched man. This is the answer to that cry.
contexts.rom-8-26: Said about the situation where a person does not know what to ask for. Paul does not advise finding the words; he says there may be no words at all.
contexts.rom-8-38: The end of a chapter that began with no condemnation. Paul lists everything he can think of, including death and the future, and closes the list.
contexts.rom-12-15: From a list of short instructions. The order matters: rejoicing with those who rejoice comes first, and it is usually harder than weeping with those who weep.
contexts.rom-12-21: The conclusion of a section on how to treat enemies. Just before it Paul quotes Proverbs and talks about food and drink for an opponent.
contexts.1co-1-27: Paul reminds the Corinthians of their own make-up: not many wise, not many well-born. He says it to a community proud of its own spirituality.
contexts.1co-15-58: The last line of the resurrection chapter, Paul's longest argument that death is not final. The conclusion turns out to be about work.
contexts.2co-9-7: From a letter about a collection for the hungry in Jerusalem. Paul spent years gathering it and stresses that compulsion ruins the whole thing.
contexts.2co-12-10: The conclusion of his account of a weakness that was not taken away. Paul lists insults and persecutions as things he is content to be in.
contexts.gal-3-28: Written in a world where those three distinctions decided everything: rights, courts, inheritance. Paul names precisely the boundaries that could not be crossed.
contexts.gal-6-2: It sits beside a line saying each will carry his own load. The Greek words differ: one means a crushing weight, the other a traveller's pack.
contexts.eph-4-2: The start of the letter's practical half. The word rendered 'bearing with' means putting up with an inconvenient person, not pardoning an offence.
contexts.eph-4-26: Anger is not forbidden here; a time limit is set on it. The measure comes from the day itself: sunset was the end of the day, not a figure of speech.
contexts.eph-5-15: The phrase rendered 'making the most of the time' literally means buying time back, the way goods are bought at market, because the days are evil.
contexts.php-3-13: Paul has just listed his past, including persecuting the church, and called all of it rubbish. The forgetting here covers both his credentials and his guilt.
contexts.php-4-11: Paul stresses that he learned contentment rather than starting out content. He names both schools he went through: being full and going hungry.
contexts.col-3-15: The verb rendered 'let rule' comes from sport: it described an umpire awarding the prize. Peace is set up as the referee inside a person.
contexts.col-4-6: Salt in that world was a preservative and a measure of value, not a spice for sharpness. The point is that words should not go bad.
contexts.1th-5-11: Said to a community expecting the end any day and jittery because of it. The instruction is plain: keep doing what you are already doing.
contexts.1ti-4-12: Written to Timothy, left in Ephesus to lead a community while being noticeably younger than the people he was leading.
contexts.1ti-6-6: Said in a section about people who treat godliness as a way to make money. The measure of sufficiency given is food and clothing, and nothing else.
contexts.2ti-4-7: The closing lines of Paul's last letter. A few verses on, in verse 13, he asks for the cloak he left at Troas: the summing-up sits among household requests.
contexts.heb-6-19: The anchor here is cast not downward but upward, behind the temple curtain. The image is deliberately inverted from the nautical one.
contexts.heb-10-24: Said to a community where people had already started staying away from meetings. The verb rendered 'spur on' means to provoke, which is a fairly sharp word.
contexts.heb-12-11: The writer openly admits that at the time it does not seem pleasant, and does not try to argue otherwise. The fruit is spoken of in the future tense.
contexts.jas-1-17: An astronomical image: heavenly bodies have phases and eclipses, and James says here there are none. The comparison is more precise than it sounds.
contexts.jas-1-19: Three instructions in order of difficulty. James writes to a community where, judging by the letter, arguing was frequent and enthusiastic.
contexts.jas-4-14: Said about people planning a year of travel and profit ahead. James does not forbid planning; he objects to certainty about tomorrow.
contexts.1pe-1-3: The opening of a letter to Christians called strangers in their own towns. The hope is called living, in contrast to an inheritance that can be lost.
contexts.1pe-3-15: Said to people who might be called in for questioning. The demand to give an answer comes together with a demand to do it gently, not triumphantly.
contexts.1pe-5-10: Peter writes 'after you have suffered a little while', without promising there will be no suffering. The word 'little' is his own assessment, from inside persecution.
contexts.2pe-3-9: An answer to people asking where the promised coming is, since nothing is happening. The delay is explained not by forgetfulness but by intent.
contexts.1jn-3-1: The verb opening the line is an exclamation: 'look'. John writes to a community some had left, explaining to those who stayed who they are.
contexts.1jn-3-18: Just before it stands a question about someone who sees a brother in need and closes his heart. The demand for action comes as the answer to that question.
contexts.1jn-4-19: A short line about sequence: ours is not first. It stands immediately after the words about fear being driven out by love.
contexts.rev-2-10: A letter to the church in Smyrna, one of only two, with Philadelphia, that receive no reproach. What they are promised is not rescue but prison and ten days of affliction.
contexts.rev-21-5: One of the few lines in the book spoken directly by the one on the throne. What is promised is not new things but the renewal of everything that exists.
contexts.gen-4-9: Cain answers a question with a question, having already killed his brother. His counter-question — am I my brother's keeper — is never directly answered in the Bible.
contexts.gen-18-14: Said after Sarah laughed behind the tent wall on hearing about a son. She is ninety, and she laughed inwardly, not out loud.
contexts.exo-4-11: An answer to Moses, who had refused four times and pleaded that he was slow of speech. After this he refuses a fifth time.
contexts.exo-17-12: While Moses kept his hands raised the battle went Israel's way, but his hands grew heavy. Aaron and Hur simply put a stone under him and held his arms up.
contexts.num-11-14: Moses says this while the people weep for meat. He goes on to ask outright to be killed if it continues, and that is recorded without softening.
contexts.deu-4-29: Said for the case when the people will already be scattered among other nations. The promise is given in advance, for the worst outcome envisaged.
contexts.jos-14-11: Spoken by Caleb at eighty-five, asking not for a quiet allotment but for the hill country where the giants live.
contexts.jdg-16-28: Samson's last prayer — blinded, shorn and put on display for mockery. Before this the book records only one prayer of his, when he was dying of thirst.
contexts.1sa-1-15: Hannah defends herself to a priest who took her for drunk: she was praying silently, only her lips moving. That was not how people prayed then.
contexts.1sa-7-12: Samuel sets up a stone and names it 'stone of help'. The marker is placed not after victory in general but at one specific spot.
contexts.2sa-9-7: David says this to the grandson of Saul, the man who hunted him for years. Mephibosheth is lame in both feet and living in someone else's house.
contexts.1ki-3-9: Solomon is offered anything he asks for, and asks not for wealth or long life but for the ability to tell things apart. He was about twenty.
contexts.1ki-17-16: The widow at Zarephath was making a last loaf for herself and her son, to eat it and die. The flour and oil did not run out until the drought ended.
contexts.1ki-19-4: Elijah asks to die under a bush in the desert, the day after the greatest victory of his life. The answer he receives is food and sleep.
contexts.2ki-4-26: The woman answers 'it is well', though her only son died in her arms that morning. She told no one until she reached the prophet.
contexts.1ch-28-20: David hands Solomon the plans for a temple he was not allowed to build himself. He says this to his son knowing he will not see the work.
contexts.2ch-16-9: Said to King Asa as a rebuke: he hired an ally instead of relying on God, and is charged not with failure but with calculation.
contexts.neh-1-4: Nehemiah is cupbearer to the Persian king and has just heard that Jerusalem's walls lie in ruins. He wept and fasted for days before doing anything.
contexts.est-4-16: Esther decides to go to the king uninvited, knowing the law. Her last words — if I perish, I perish — are not hope but consent to the outcome.
contexts.job-2-10: An answer to his wife, who suggested cursing God and dying. Job at that moment is sitting in ashes, scraping himself with a shard of pottery.
contexts.job-14-1: Job speaks about human life in general, in the middle of an argument about his own. The images are from nature: a flower and a shadow, both short-lived.
contexts.job-29-2: Job remembers how things used to be, in the one chapter of the book given entirely to longing for the past. He is not asking for it back; he is listing it.
contexts.psa-5-3: A morning psalm of David. The verb rendered 'lay before you' comes from sacrificial practice: it described arranging wood at daybreak.
contexts.psa-6-6: David writes that he wears himself out with groaning through the night and drenches his bed with tears. The psalm is classed as penitential, but its complaint is bodily.
contexts.psa-9-9: The word rendered 'high tower' means a height that cannot be reached from below. This psalm and the next together form one acrostic; the Greek Bible counts them as a single psalm.
contexts.psa-17-8: Two images in a row: the pupil of an eye, protected without thinking, and a bird tucking its young under a wing. Both are drawn from reflex, not from choice.
contexts.psa-18-28: The psalm was written the day David escaped from Saul. The lamp here is the same small clay lamp the app is named after.
contexts.psa-24-1: A psalm for entering the temple, sung at the gates. The claim that the whole earth belongs to God was spoken just before stepping onto one small plot.
contexts.psa-41-1: The psalm of a sick man who writes that visitors come and lie to his face. The line about caring for the poor stands at the start, before the complaint.
contexts.psa-50-15: A psalm where God declines sacrifices, explaining that he is not hungry. Instead of meat he asks for thanksgiving and a call in trouble.
contexts.psa-57-1: The heading places this psalm when David was hiding in a cave from Saul. The shadow of wings is a bird image, not an architectural one.
contexts.psa-70-5: A short psalm made entirely of a request to hurry. The last words in the Hebrew are 'do not delay', and there it breaks off.
contexts.psa-78-4: The opening of the longest historical psalm. It goes on to retell the people's failures honestly too: the task is to pass things on, not to improve them.
contexts.psa-82-3: A psalm accusing judges of ruling unjustly and favouring the powerful. The demand is addressed to those who hold the power to decide.
contexts.psa-84-5: A pilgrim's psalm. The Hebrew speaks of people who have the roads in their hearts: they pass through a valley of weeping and turn it into a spring.
contexts.psa-92-14: A psalm for the sabbath. A botanical image: date palms and cedars bear more the older they get, and every listener knew it.
contexts.psa-115-1: A psalm from the Passover cycle that opens by refusing credit. It goes on to mock idols that have eyes and ears which do not work.
contexts.psa-117-1: The shortest psalm in the Psalter, two lines long. Yet it addresses all nations rather than Israel, which is rare for the Psalter.
contexts.psa-119-130: From the longest psalm, an acrostic about the law. The verb rendered 'unfolding' literally means an opening, the way a door is opened and light falls in.
contexts.psa-150-6: The final line of the whole Psalter, after a hundred and forty-nine psalms that included curses and complaints about God's silence.
contexts.pro-6-6: The advice to look at the ant is given to a sluggard. The argument rests on the ant having neither commander nor overseer, and the work getting done anyway.
contexts.pro-13-12: A saying about what deferred waiting does to a person physically. Both images are bodily: a sick heart and a tree of life.
contexts.pro-17-17: The saying distinguishes a friend from a brother: the first loves at all times, the second is for trouble specifically. They are not synonyms but two different cases.
contexts.pro-25-11: From a collection compiled by King Hezekiah's men. A jeweller's image: golden fruit in a silver setting, an expensive thing made exactly to measure.
contexts.pro-28-13: A saying about two ways of handling guilt: cover it or name it. The verb for 'covers' is the same one Genesis uses for Adam hiding.
contexts.pro-30-8: A rare prayer in a book of sayings. The author asks for neither poverty nor riches and explains both risks: forgetting when full, stealing when in need.
contexts.ecc-7-3: The author advises going to a house of mourning rather than a house of feasting. His reason is practical: there you see how it ends for everyone.
contexts.sng-2-11: An invitation to come out after winter, from a book about two lovers. In that land the rains came in winter, and their end ended the staying indoors.
contexts.isa-45-3: Said about Cyrus, a Persian king who did not know Israel's God. The promise of treasures in darkness is made to an outsider, not to one of their own.
contexts.isa-60-1: Addressed to a city lying in ruins. The command to rise and shine is given to one who has no light of its own; the source is named in the next line.
contexts.isa-64-8: A line from a corporate prayer of repentance where the people admit they have all withered like a leaf. The clay image stresses dependence, not humility.
contexts.isa-66-13: The book's final chapter. A maternal comparison is rare in the prophets, and it comes right at the end, after sixty-five chapters in a different register.
contexts.jer-2-13: The prophet names two evils in a row, the second being cisterns that will not hold water. In a country without rivers that was the costliest and most galling mistake.
contexts.jer-8-22: The balm of Gilead was a well-known medicine carried by caravans. The question is rhetorical and bitter: the medicine exists, the healing does not.
contexts.jer-18-6: Jeremiah is sent to a workshop to watch someone work. The pot went wrong in the potter's hands, so he made another from the same clay: that is the whole lesson.
contexts.jer-20-9: Jeremiah has just spent a night in the stocks and declared he would prophesy no more. This is his admission of why staying silent did not work.
contexts.jer-31-25: After this line the prophet adds that he woke and his sleep had been sweet. It is the only place in the book where he mentions his own sleep.
contexts.lam-3-31: From the lament over ruined Jerusalem. It says God does not afflict people from the willingness of his heart — that is, not willingly.
contexts.ezk-22-30: God says he looked for someone to stand in the breach of the wall and found no one. The line ends with the search having failed.
contexts.dan-2-22: Daniel says this at night, after the king's dream was revealed to him. The execution of all Babylon's wise men had already been ordered, himself included.
contexts.hos-6-6: Jesus quotes this line twice in arguments about whom one may eat with and what may be done on the sabbath. In Hosea it is said about formal worship.
contexts.jol-2-28: The prophecy lists those who normally received no word: sons and daughters, the old, the young, male and female slaves. The list itself is the news.
contexts.jon-4-2: Jonah explains why he ran: he knew from the start the city would be spared. It is precisely the mercy he is angry about, nothing else.
contexts.mic-4-4: The image of peace is not a palace but one's own vine and fig tree, with no one to cause fear. The prophet's measure of wellbeing is entirely domestic.
contexts.hag-2-4: Said to the builders of the second temple, who are being told by the old that the first was incomparably better. The instruction is simple: be strong and work.
contexts.zec-9-12: The phrase 'prisoners of hope' is a deliberate paradox: the people are still captive, and hope is named as what holds them, not what freed them.
contexts.mat-5-44: From the Sermon on the Mount. The listeners lived under Roman occupation, so 'enemy' meant specific armed people to them, not an abstraction.
contexts.mat-11-29: Said in Galilee to those who have run out of strength. A yoke was put on a pair: the young animal learned by walking beside a grown one, not alone.
contexts.mat-18-21: Peter proposes forgiving seven times, thinking it generous: the rabbis of the day spoke of three. The answer moves the count into a range where counting is pointless.
contexts.mat-23-37: Said over the city at the end of a speech of rebuke. The image of a hen with chicks breaks the tone abruptly, and it ends with the words 'you were not willing'.
contexts.mat-26-41: Said to disciples who fell asleep in the garden while he prayed. Luke adds that they slept from grief rather than from carelessness.
contexts.mrk-2-17: An answer to scribes outraged that he was eating with tax collectors. The argument is medical, and it was spoken at the table of one of them.
contexts.mrk-9-23: An answer to the father who said 'if you can'. Jesus hands the 'if' back to him, and the father's next line becomes the most honest answer in the Gospels.
contexts.mrk-14-8: Said about a woman who poured expensive perfume over his head. Those present were indignant at the waste; he measured not the amount but the timing.
contexts.luk-2-19: Said of Mary the night the shepherds came with their account of angels. Everyone else marvelled aloud; she said nothing and stored it up.
contexts.luk-22-32: Said to Peter before the denial, not after. Jesus does not promise he will not fall; he says he prayed for his faith, and gives him a task for afterwards.
contexts.luk-22-61: Peter denies him a third time, a cock crows, and Jesus, being led across the courtyard, turns and looks at him. No words are exchanged.
contexts.jhn-2-5: Mary's last words in the Gospels, said to servants at a wedding where the wine ran out. She says nothing further in John's Gospel.
contexts.jhn-5-6: The question is put to a man who had lain by the pool for thirty-eight years. He does not answer yes; he explains why it never works out.
contexts.jhn-13-7: An answer to Peter, who refused to let his feet be washed. The promise of understanding is placed in the future, not given on the spot.
contexts.jhn-14-18: The word rendered 'orphans' literally means bereaved of a parent. Said to disciples hours before they lose him.
contexts.jhn-19-30: The last word from the cross in John's Gospel, a single word in Greek. It was used on receipts to mark a debt paid in full.
contexts.jhn-20-15: Mary weeps at the empty tomb and takes him for the gardener. She recognises him not by sight but when he says her name.
contexts.act-3-6: Peter answers a beggar at the temple gate who had asked for money. He begins by admitting he has none, and only then offers something else.
contexts.act-14-22: Paul says this having returned to a city where shortly before he had been stoned and dragged outside the walls, presumed dead.
contexts.act-28-15: Paul is being taken to Rome under guard, and Roman Christians walk many miles out to meet him. Luke notes that on seeing them Paul took courage.
contexts.rom-5-3: A chain of four links with affliction first. Paul does not say affliction is good; he describes what grows out of it when it is endured.
contexts.rom-12-1: A deliberately contradictory phrase: a sacrifice is by definition dead, and here it is called living. This is how the letter's practical half begins.
contexts.1co-3-6: Paul is addressing a split in a community where some called themselves his followers and others Apollos'. He divides the work into stages to remove the grounds for arguing.
contexts.1co-12-26: From the comparison of a community to a body. The argument is physiological: pain in one place is felt by the whole organism, and goodwill has nothing to do with it.
contexts.1co-13-12: Mirrors of that time were polished bronze and gave a blurred reflection. The image is about the quality of sight, not about distance.
contexts.1co-15-10: Paul has just called himself the least of the apostles and unworthy of the name, because he persecuted the church. The line about grace answers his own charge.
contexts.2co-4-7: Clay jars were the cheapest containers, not worth regretting if broken. The contrast between contents and packaging is the whole point.
contexts.2co-5-7: A short line inside an argument that what is seen is temporary. The contrast is not between faith and reason but between faith and sight.
contexts.2co-7-6: Paul writes that in Macedonia he had no rest and was pressed on every side. The comfort came not through a revelation but through a person arriving: Titus.
contexts.gal-6-7: An agricultural image, entirely everyday: what is sown is what grows, regardless of intentions. Said at the end of a sharp letter.
contexts.eph-2-10: The word rendered 'workmanship' is the Greek root of 'poem'. The line comes right after the statement that salvation is not by works.
contexts.php-2-14: The instruction comes straight after the hymn about Christ emptying himself. The demand not to grumble is set out as the conclusion drawn from that hymn.
contexts.col-3-12: The verb 'clothe yourselves' is about garments put on deliberately each morning. Just before, the old self is described as something taken off like a robe.
contexts.1th-5-14: Three groups and three different approaches: warn the idle, comfort the fainthearted, hold up the weak. Paul distinguishes who needs what.
contexts.2th-3-3: It comes right after the admission that not everyone has faith. The statement about God's faithfulness is set against the unreliability of people.
contexts.1ti-1-15: Paul calls himself the foremost of sinners in the present tense, not the past. He then explains that this is exactly why he was shown mercy: as an example.
contexts.2ti-2-13: The last line of an early Christian hymn that Paul quotes. Of the four lines it alone breaks the symmetry: the response is not a mirror.
contexts.2ti-4-17: Paul writes that at his first hearing no one came and everyone deserted him. He asks that it not be held against them, and says who did stand by.
contexts.heb-2-18: The argument rests on experience: help comes from one who has been through it. The verb rendered 'tempted' here means being tested to the limit, not enticed.
contexts.heb-13-2: An allusion to Abraham receiving three travellers by the oaks, and to Lot. The point is that neither knew whom he was receiving; otherwise the argument fails.
contexts.jas-2-17: Just before comes an example: someone without clothes or food is told 'go in peace, keep warm' and given nothing. The conclusion is drawn from that example.
contexts.jas-4-6: A quotation from Proverbs cited in the middle of an analysis of quarrels in the community. James explains where the fighting comes from, and finds the cause in desires.
contexts.jas-5-7: The image of a farmer waiting for rain. That land had two rain seasons, early and late, and between them nothing was left but waiting.
contexts.1pe-4-8: The next line explains what this looks like in practice: take one another in without grumbling. These were people living close together and poor.
contexts.1pe-5-8: Peter writes to the persecuted and adds that the same is happening to their brothers throughout the world. The comfort here is that they are not alone in it.
contexts.1jn-3-20: This is about the case where a person's own heart accuses them. John does not argue with the accusation; he says there is a court higher than the heart.
contexts.jud-1-24: The closing lines of a short letter, given over almost entirely to warnings about deception. It ends not with a threat but with a promise to hold someone up.
contexts.rev-1-17: John writes that he fell as though dead at the vision. The first thing he hears is not an explanation but 'do not be afraid', with a hand on him.
contexts.rev-7-17: Said about people who came out of great tribulation. The image is deliberately inverted: the lamb is called the shepherd who leads to springs of water.
contexts.rev-14-13: One of the few places in the book where a voice orders something written down separately. Said of those who died under persecution: rest is named first, their deeds follow after.
contexts.rev-22-5: The book's second-to-last image. Night is named as what will no longer exist, and with it the need for a lamp, where the whole thing began.
